summary: Documents a process to apply architectural discipline to future development of the Session Initiation Protocol, responding to concerns that new features could harm security or add complexity. It sets out how proposals are reviewed. It was replaced by RFC 5727.

eli5.summary: SIP kept getting extra features, and too many could make it messy. This note sets up a gate so new ideas get checked before they join. It was later replaced by RFC 5727.

questions: what is the sipping working group
subtitle: The IETF's gatekeeping rules for extending SIP, including the "P-" header escape hatch.

tldr.problem: SIP became popular and attracted a flood of suggestions for changes and extensions. Too many features could damage security and greatly increase the protocol's complexity.
tldr.mechanism: Requirements go first through the SIPPING working group, and only the SIP working group may then change SIP. Experimental or special-purpose headers can be registered as "P-" headers under strict conditions, and event packages follow their own rules.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice has been obsoleted by RFC 5727 and updated by RFC 3968 and RFC 3969, so it is no longer the current SIP change process.

facts.label: Registries
facts.value: SIP methods, option tags, response codes, headers, event packages

today: RFC 3427 has been obsoleted by RFC 5727, and it was also updated by RFC 3968 and RFC 3969. Read it as the history of how SIP changes were first gated; RFC 5727 is the replacement.

sections.title: Why SIP Needed a Change Process
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) was first developed to start multimedia sessions. Internet multimedia, voice over IP and IP telephony grew popular, inside the IETF and with other standards groups, and the uses of SIP grew with them. One result was a continual flood of suggestions for SIP modifications and extensions.

The abstract names the worry: adding new SIP features can be damaging to security and can greatly increase the complexity of the protocol. The job of IETF management was to keep SIP development focused on the core strengths of SIP and the applications it does best.
sections.eli5: Lots of people wanted to add things to SIP. If everything gets added, the protocol becomes tangled and easier to break, so someone has to say no sometimes.

sections.title: The SIP and SIPPING Working Groups
sections.content:
The IETF SIP Working Group is chartered to be the owner and guardian of SIP for as long as the group exists. All changes or extensions to SIP must first exist as SIP Working Group documents, and the group should only change SIP when there are compelling reasons. New SIP methods, option tags, response codes and new standards track SIP headers must be handled by this group. With the exception of "P-" headers, all SIP extensions must be standards track.

The SIPPING Working Group is chartered to be a filter in front of the SIP group. It investigates requirements for applications of SIP and may decide that SIP already satisfies them, that they are not general enough to warrant a change, that they justify a change, or that they should be combined with other requirements. It should accept only requirements that play to the best strengths of SIP, such as realtime presence, and reject uses such as controlling household appliances just because SIP is there.

If these groups have closed, the Transport Area directors use the non-working group standards track process from RFC 2026 with the SIP and SIPPING mailing lists and designated experts for advice. The IETF stays the home of SIP extensions.
sections.eli5: One group listens to ideas and asks whether SIP is really the right tool. A second group decides how, or whether, to change SIP itself. It is like a teacher who checks an idea before it goes to the principal.

sections.title: The SIP Change Process
sections.content:
Anyone who thinks SIP fits their application but is not sufficient must write an individual Internet-Draft. It must explain the problem, why SIP is the applicable protocol and why existing SIP will not work. It must include a detailed set of requirements, distinct from solutions, and describe in detail any security issues that arise from meeting them. The authors then send a note to the SIPPING mailing list to start discussion.

The SIPPING chairs, together with the Transport Area Directors, decide from the discussion whether the problem should be added to the SIPPING charter. If both agree, the directors present the charter change to the IESG and IAB. If the IESG approves, with IAB advice, SIPPING can work on the problem.

The authors may describe the SIP changes that would meet the requirements in a separate Internet-Draft, which goes to the SIP Working Group if warranted. That group is not required to adopt the proposed solution, and it must protect the architectural integrity of SIP. It must not add features without general use beyond the specific case, or add features just to make one function more efficient at the expense of simplicity or robustness. SIP extensions come only from the IETF, and the IETF will not publish a SIP extension RFC outside these processes.
sections.eli5: First you write down the problem and why you need it, not just your favourite fix. A group checks it, then another group decides whether to change SIP, and they can still say no.

sections.title: P- Headers and Event Packages
sections.content:
Some extensions may not be ready for standards track, or may be private or proprietary. These can use "P-" headers, where the P stands for preliminary, private or proprietary. An informational header can be registered as a "P-" header only if all of these hold: a designated expert reviews it; it defines no option tags, response codes or methods; it does not overlap with chartered extensions; it is purely informational and does not significantly change the behavior of SIP entities; it does not undermine SIP security and the Internet-Draft covers security as for a Standards Track document; it is documented in an Informational RFC and registered with IANA; and an applicability statement explains its limited scope.

An implementation of a "P-" header MUST include the "P-" prefix, as in P-Headername. Such extensions are not IETF standards, and MUST NOT be required by any production deployment considered compliant to IETF specifications. Unknown P-headers are ignored. Any P-header used outside a very restricted research or teaching environment MUST meet the requirements and MUST be documented in an RFC and registered with IANA.

The same RFC also sets rules for SIP event packages. Event template-packages can only be created by a Standards Track RFC from an IETF working group. Normal event packages can come from any chartered working group RFC, or from an individual Informational RFC after SIPPING review, an expert review and conditions that mirror the ones for P-headers.
sections.eli5: P- headers are like a sticky note with a P on it that says this is a trial idea, not an official rule. Everyone may ignore it, and nobody may depend on it.

sections.title: IANA Registration Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3261 directs IANA to keep registries for SIP method names, option tags and response codes, and to amend the existing registry for SIP headers. Apart from P-headers, an entry goes in only when an Internet-Draft is approved as a standards track RFC. Registration happens when the IESG announces approval of the draft.

Standard headers and messages MUST NOT begin with P-, and P-header names MUST begin with it. No P-header may conflict with the name of an existing standards track header without the prefix. Each registration also reserves the unprefixed name, which MUST NOT be used in an implementation before the header is standardized. Short forms of headers MUST only be assigned to standards track headers, so P-headers MUST NOT have short forms.

For event packages, RFC 3265 directs IANA to keep a registry. Template packages need an approved standards track draft, and ordinary packages need an approved draft for an RFC of any type.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official list of names. Experimental names get a P in front so they can never be mistaken for an official name, and the official version of the name stays saved for later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that complexity, and protocol behavior that is hard to define because it depends on which of many extensions operate, is a fine breeding ground for security flaws.

All Internet-Drafts presenting new requirements for SIP must discuss the security requirements and implications of the proposal. All RFCs that modify or extend SIP must show that they have adequate security and do not worsen the existing security considerations of SIP.
sections.eli5: A machine with too many parts is easier to break. So anyone who wants to add a part has to show it will not make the machine less safe.
